newsitem.title: POLAND: Solidarity wants Gdansk yard talks with Polish PM.
newsitem.headline: Solidarity wants Gdansk yard talks with Polish PM.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity trade union on Wednesday demanded talks with Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on ways to save the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, the organisation's birthplace.
"We should explain who is to be blamed and why agreements regarding the yard have not been implemented," Solidarity chairman Marian Krzaklewski told reporters after meeting with the yard's workers.

He said the union would consider protest action unless the government took measures to save the shipyard, where 17 years ago Lech Walesa founded Solidarity, the then Soviet bloc's first free trade union.
The yard appeared to be heading for collapse after a consortium of banks refused it a $100 million loan on Tuesday to finance construction of five ships for a German contractor.

Solidarity and the yard's workers are bitter at the government because its officials repeatedly said the company's bankruptcy last year was a prelude to its restructuring and revival and not to its disappearance.
The German contract would have kept part of the yard alive while the government and the yard's management sought an investor to save the business.
The shipyard has operated on bankruptcy regulations since August last year, when its debts reached 415 million zlotys ($136 million) and banks refused further credit.
Its workforce, mostly idled, is gradually shrinking.
The government, grouping ex-communists and a peasant party, blames the shipyard's previous managements, supported by Solidarity, for the company's misfortunes.

Solidarity, which helped topple communist rule in 1989, says the government has offered subsidies to other state-owned companies and is denying them to the shipyard because it is a centre of opposition.
A Solidarity-led electoral bloc hopes to defeat the ex-communists, sharing power with the Peasant Party since 1993, in parliamentary elections due around September.
